The Guerrilla speaks
2013-03-25T00:15:27+06:00 | Shah Alam Shazu
https://www.thedailystar.net/news/the-guerrilla-speaks

Photo: ATL Aakash

Nasiruddin Yousuff, a valiant guerrilla fighter during the Liberation War, is also an eminent cultural personality and a key figure behind the renowned Dhaka Theatre. He has also garnered much acclaim both in the country and abroad for directing the film “

Guerrilla

”. Yousuff also hosted the show “

Muktijuddho Protidin

” to help disseminate true stories of brave freedom fighters.

The Daily Star recently met up with Yousuff at his Purana Paltan residence, where he shared his personal experiences and thoughts.

The first movie you directed was

“Ekatturer Jishu”

. Tell us about the experience.

Nasiruddin Yousuff:

It was a timely movie. Author Shahriar Kabir and I started working on the project when the

Gono Adalat

(People's Court) was formed. We selected Shahriar Kabir's novel for the story, while additional help was provided by David Pranab Das.

“Ekatturer Jishu”

had a lot of passion and emotion in it. Baby Islam was behind the camera. However, I was not completely satisfied with the film.

What about “Guerrilla”?

Nasiruddin Yousuff:

“

Guerrilla

” was also what the time demanded. From a technical point of view, it's better than

“Ekatturer Jishu”

. “

Guerrilla

” also exceeds its predecessor in many aspects. I think “

Guerrilla

” manages to capture the epic proportion of the story better. It was based on true events.

“Guerrilla” picked up National Film Awards in 10 different categories, as well as being admired by the masses. How was all this possible?

Nasiruddin Yousuff:

“

Guerrilla

” had been shown at

Gono Jagoron Moncho

several times, where people responded with great admiration. The film was also shown around the country, including in the most remote regions, and it drew praise from people from all communities. All the love and interest shown by the people towards the film is a great achievement for me; not only as a director, but also as a freedom fighter. The National Awards are also a great achievement. This recognition will definitely inspire the cast and crew of the movie and encourage me to make better films in the future. “

Guerrilla

” has also been shown at several major festivals around the country, along with bagging a few awards. I believe that these are all the outcome of the love I have for my work.

Tell us about the show you are hosting -- “

Muktijuddho Protidin

”.

Nasiruddin Yousuff:

Over 2,000 freedom fighters,

Birangonas

and family members of the martyrs have appeared on the show so far. The audience gets to hear their experiences during 1971. Viewers get to listen to true stories of suffering and the brutalities committed during the war. I travelled to many places in the country for this show and talked to many freedom fighters and common people. I also received the love and support of many over the course of the show. I've been able to unmask the viciousness of the

Razakars

and

al-Badr

members through this show.

Would you share with us some of your personal experiences of March 1971?

Nasiruddin Yousuff:

We celebrated

Potaka Uttolon Dibosh

(the day the national flag was hoisted) on March 23. On that day, we hoisted the flag at Bangabandhu

's

residence. With the ongoing situation as the backdrop, we were getting prepared. We didn't have any weapon at the time, and had no idea how dangerous it would be to stay unarmed while facing an army. On March 25, we returned at around 8pm, after spending the day in front of Bangabandhu

's

house. Thousands of people went there during the day. At 8:30pm, we received a letter from Sergeant Zahurul Haq Hall, instructing us to build defences in our own areas. Some friends and I were assigned to create barricades on the road. On that night, we created barricades on different roads of Paltan by placing pipes on the street.

Later at 11:45pm, the Pakistan army started firing bullets near the current Kakrail Mosque at a rate that we had never experienced before. We didn't know at that time that they were moving towards Rajarbag. They broke our barricades on their way. That was the first time I saw tanks. I had no idea that the sound of gunshots could be so loud. Within a short period of time, many houses in our area were blown away under the army's bombardment. At around 1am, we heard sounds of massive gunfire from the Rajarbag area. They went there with the intent of finishing off the Bengali policemen.

At around 4 in the morning, many policemen -- some naked, some with minimal clothing -- came in front of our Paltan residence and asked for clothes. We provided them with clothing and food, and kept their weapons. They told us how many other policemen were killed during the night. At early dawn, I peeked on the street to see that army men were patrolling the road in front of Jonaki cinema hall. I also peeked towards the house of a friend to see that many corpses were lying there, including burnt bodies. It was a horrible day, followed by a similarly horrible March 26 night.

On March 25, we also saw smoke coming from the direction of Dhaka University and old Dhaka. Corpses were everywhere. I had never before seen thousands of dead bodies. The curfew was lifted for a few hours on the morning of March 27. During that time, some friends and I crossed the river, taking with us seven guns left behind by the policemen. We thought of fighting from over there to recapture Dhaka.

I was a Dhaka University student during March 1971. The brutality of March 26 transformed me and many more like me overnight, and inspired us to take up arms. That one night changed us into freedom fighters, and made us stand against the mass killings. The month of March prepared the nation to fight within a moment's notice.
